stops.name: Basra, her father's house, the night of no oil
stops.campa: In a poor house of Basra a fourth daughter is born, and there is not one drop of oil in the house to anoint her navel, no lamp, no rag to swaddle her in. Her father, sworn by covenant never to beg of any mortal, will not even ask the neighbor for oil; his wife weeps. He sleeps and dreams the Prophet, who tells him the girl is a queen among women, intercessor for seventy thousand of his people, and sends him to the governor of Basra for four hundred lawful dinars. He wakes weeping, and writes as he was bidden.
stops.quote: The girl child who has just come to earth is a queen among women, who shall be the intercessor for seventy thousand of my community.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. A. J. Arberry, Muslim Saints and Mystics

stops.name: Basra, the famine, and the six dirhams
stops.campa: Rabia is still young when her mother and father die and a famine falls on Basra; her three sisters are scattered to the winds of want. Venturing into the streets for bread, she is seen by a wicked man who seizes the orphaned girl and sells her in the market for six dirhams, a price the tradition never lets her or her hearers forget. Her purchaser sets her to hard labor by day. Nothing yet marks her as a queen among women except the covenant her father swore, which she now unknowingly inherits: to ask nothing of any creature.

stops.name: Basra, the road, the fall, and the broken hand
stops.campa: Passing along a Basra road on some errand of her master's, Rabia sees a strange man approach and flees him. She falls headlong; her hand is dislocated in the fall. Bowing her face to the ground where she lies, a slave, an orphan, a stranger with a broken hand, she does not ask to be spared the fall's pain, only whether God is pleased with her or not. A voice answers her out of the ground itself, promising a station envied by the cherubim of heaven. She rises and returns to her master's house unhealed but unafraid.
stops.quote: Lord God, I am a stranger, orphaned of mother and father, a helpless prisoner fallen into captivity, my hand broken. Yet for all this I do not grieve; all I need is Thy good pleasure, to know whether Thou art well-pleased or no.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, the master's window, the lantern without a chain
stops.campa: By day Rabia fasts and serves; by night she stands in prayer until dawn, telling God that if the choice were hers she would never rest an hour from His service, only He has set her under the hand of a creature. One night her master wakes, looks through the window, and sees her bowing in prayer beneath a lantern hung with no chain, its light filling the whole house. Afraid, he sits pondering until morning, then calls her, is gentle with her, and sets her free. She asks only his leave to go, and receives it.
stops.quote: O God, Thou knowest that the desire of my heart is in conformity with Thy command, and that the light of my eye is in serving Thy court. If the affair lay with me, I would not rest one hour from serving Thee, but Thou Thyself hast set me under the hand of a creature.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Beyond Basra, the desert, the leaving of the house
stops.campa: Freed, Rabia does not seek a husband, a trade, or a patron among the pious of Basra who would gladly have taken in so marked a girl. She walks out past the last walls and gardens into the waste places, carrying nothing that binds her to a roof. The desert that swallows caravans and unmakes travelers receives her instead as a threshold. She has already, in her master's house, learned to want only one thing; the desert simply removes every other thing that could be wanted, leaving her the room in which to want it without division.

stops.name: A hermitage in the wilderness, the covenant of forty years
stops.campa: From the desert Rabia comes to a hermitage and settles to serve God there, alone, for what will become the rest of her long life. Here she binds herself by a vow the tradition will quote for forty years running: never to ask anything of any but Him. No neighbor's oil, no borrowed onion, no patron's purse will move her from this line, however plain her hunger or bare her house. The hermitage has no address the geographers keep, only the fact of it: a woman, a mat, a jar, and a covenant harder than the walls around her.
stops.quote: Forty years now I have had a covenant with Almighty God not to ask for aught of any but He.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Basra, setting her face toward the desert road
stops.campa: In time Rabia determines to perform the pilgrimage, the duty owed once in a life to the House at Mecca. She binds her small bundle onto an ass and sets out from Basra along the desert road the pilgrim caravans keep, the same sands Basra's governors have dug wells along since the city's founding. She travels as she has lived, refusing company that would carry her burden for her, trusting the road to the same Providence that fed her onions and freed her from a lantern's witness. The house of God lies many hundred miles across the waste ahead.

stops.name: Wadi al-Batin, the ass dies in the heart of the desert
stops.campa: At Wadi al-Batin, where the Basra road cuts into the emptiest of the desert crossing, Rabia's ass falls dead beneath its load. The men of the party offer to carry her bundle for her; she refuses them outright, having not set out trusting in men. Left alone in the waste, she lifts her face and asks whether kings treat a stranger and powerless woman so, invited to His house only to be abandoned in the road's middle with a dead beast for company. She does not curse the desert; she simply asks the House to answer for it.
stops.quote: O God, do kings so treat a woman who is a stranger and powerless? Thou hast invited me unto Thy house, then in the midst of the way Thou hast suffered my ass to die, leaving me alone in the desert.
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: The Ad-Dahna sands, the ass revived, the mountain and Moses
stops.campa: Her prayer scarcely finished, the dead ass stirs and rises; she loads her bundle again and goes on into the red dunes of the Dahna, the hardest belt of the whole crossing. Days later, spent, she halts and cries that her heart is weary, that she is only clay walking toward a house of stone, and that she needs Him here, now, not at the end of so much sand. God answers unmediated in her heart: she fares in the life-blood of eighteen thousand worlds; let her recall how Moses begged the vision and a mountain shattered for less.
stops.quote: Rabia, thou art faring in the life-blood of eighteen thousand worlds. Hast thou not seen how Moses prayed for the vision of Me? And I cast a few motes of revelation upon the mountain, and the mountain shivered into forty pieces. Be content here with My name!
stops.quote_source: Farid al-Din Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, tr. Arberry

stops.name: Outskirts of Mecca, Ibrahim ibn Adham and the wandering Kaaba
stops.campa: Ibrahim ibn Adham, prince turned beggar, has spent fourteen years crossing this same desert on foot, praying two prostrations at every step, to reach the House. He arrives at last to find the Kaaba gone from its place, and a voice tells him it has moved to go and meet a woman who approaches. He runs and finds Rabia arriving, and the House already back on its foundation behind her. Fourteen years of prostrations, and a woman he has never met has drawn the House itself out to the road to greet her before he could finish his approach.
stops.quote: You have spent fourteen years in crossing the desert in ritual prayer; I have crossed it in personal supplication.
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition (recorded in later redactions of Attar and Jami's Nafahat al-Uns)

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba, 'the Lord of the house whom I need'
stops.campa: Rabia comes to the Kaaba at last, the black-draped House that has, the tradition says, come out on the road to meet her before she has even finished the last stage. She will not be satisfied with a building, however holy, however far she has walked to it. She circles it and speaks the sentence that becomes her name in every later telling of this scene: it is the Lord of the House she needs, not the House; stone has no power over her; only the promise that whoever approaches by a span will be met by a cubit answers her.
stops.quote: It is the Lord of the house whom I need, what have I to do with the house? I need to meet with Him Who said, 'Who approaches Me by a span's length, I will approach him by the length of a cubit.'
stops.quote_source: Sufi hagiographic tradition (recorded in later redactions of Attar and Jami's Nafahat al-Uns)

stops.name: Basra, the return from the pilgrimage
stops.campa: The pilgrimage made, the vow discharged, Rabia turns back across the same desert road toward Basra and the hermitage she left. She brings back no relic, no souvenir of the House, only the sentence she spoke at it, which will outlast every stone of Mecca in the mouths of those who tell her story. She resumes the narrow life of fasting and night-prayer exactly where she set it down, as though the whole outward journey had been folded invisibly into the stillness she never really left. Basra receives her back as the same poor woman who departed, and greater.
